item.description: That algae does more than provide food—it ultimately helps create the color flamingos are known for. Carotenoid pigments acquired through their diet are metabolized and deposited in their feathers, producing those pink and reddish tones. Live by the Elements Fuente: National Geographic.

item.description: Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: LST-1 and MAGIC telescopes shatter distance record for the very high-energy blazar OP 313
item.description: On Aug. 15, the CTAO LST Collaboration and the MAGIC Collaboration released findings from observations of OP 313, the most distant very-high-energy blazar ever recorded. The paper, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, presents in-depth observations conducted with the prototype Large-Sized Telescope (LST-1) and the MAGIC telescopes at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory in La Palma, Spain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reframing Homer's Sirens through gender, nature and social order
item.description: Though they are pivotal to Homer's epic, luring Odysseus with the promise of eternal wisdom, the Greek poet barely described the mysterious Sirens. What might a better understanding of these formless, disembodied feminine creatures contribute to this timeless teaching myth? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How chromosomes find their partners
item.description: For a long time, so-called satellite DNA was considered largely worthless. Now, ETH Zurich researchers have shown in fruit flies that these repetitive sections of genetic material act as a kind of barcode, enabling the correct chromosomes to recognize one another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flamingo remind us how deeply life is shaped by place. Their lives are shaped by the waters that sustain them, and in turn, their presence is part of the living story of that…
item.description: Flamingo remind us how deeply life is shaped by place. Their lives are shaped by the waters that sustain them, and in turn, their presence is part of the living story of that place. Organization of Nature Evolutionaries ONE Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Scientists identify design rules for the best thermoelectric materials
item.description: Researchers from Tokyo Metropolitan University have used a theoretical framework to derive design rules for creating new thermoelectric materials. The efficiency of converting thermal energy to electricity is often determined by parameters that strongly depend on each other, making it difficult to identify ideal recipes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: GenAI cannot accurately grade student essays in higher education, study finds
item.description: New research from Cardiff University and the University of Melbourne has investigated whether GenAI could mimic human marking when evaluating written student work. The results have been published in the journal Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 1998, Costa Rica spread 12,000 tonnes of orange waste; 16 years later, forest biomass rose 176%
item.description: In 1998, about 12,000 metric tonnes of orange peels and pulp were spread over a degraded pasture in Costa Rica as part of an unusual forest restoration experiment. Sixteen years later, researchers found that the site had developed into a dense forest, with richer soil, greater tree diversity and a 176% increase in aboveground biomass. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: New free-space optical link adds a wireless component to the nation's longest quantum network
item.description: There's a new lighthouse on Long Island. But instead of shining light to guide ships through waterways, this one transmits and receives particles of light that carry quantum information. Perched atop a seven-story building at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Brookhaven National Laboratory, the "Quantum Lighthouse" is a key pillar of the free-space optical (FSO) link spanning Brookhaven Lab, the State University of New York at Stony Brook (Stony Brook University) and Yale University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Long-term study reveals hidden threat of schistosomiasis in endangered chimpanzees
item.description: A 12-year study of rescued chimpanzees at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary (NICS) in Uganda has revealed persistent intestinal schistosomiasis infections, highlighting the need for long-term disease surveillance to protect endangered wildlife. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dry landscapes and newly fallowed fields may raise California Valley fever risk
item.description: Researchers at UC San Diego and UC Berkeley have found that certain landscapes surrounding California communities are associated with differing rates of Valley fever, a fungal respiratory infection caused by inhaling spores carried in windblown dust. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Meet Dai Zheng, the space veteran betting on China’s reusable rocket revolution
item.description: Ten years ago, Dai Zheng made a career-defining gamble: he left his secure, prestigious engineering post in China’s state space programme to join an unproven private start-up. On August 19, that risk paid off when a rocket booster returned from orbit and landed upright for the first time in Chinese commercial space history. For Dai, now chief commander of the Zhuque-3 missions at LandSpace, the successful touchdown marked both a major personal milestone and a critical leap forward in China’s... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ben Jiang

item.title: Immigration can bring small overall gains but uneven wage effects
item.description: Immigration can produce a small economic gain for the native-born population overall while causing larger shifts in wages between different groups of workers, according to new research co-authored by King's Business School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Common medications may change your gut for years
item.description: Common medications may reshape the gut microbiome long after the last dose is taken. In a study of more than 2,500 people, researchers found lasting microbial changes linked not only to antibiotics, but also to antidepressants, beta-blockers, acid-reducing drugs, and benzodiazepines. Some effects were still detectable years later, suggesting past medication use may strongly influence the gut bacteria people carry today. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A 4-star system caught eclipsing itself in a way never seen before
item.description: Astronomers have found a four-star system doing something that has never been confirmed before. The system, TIC 433545934, has two close pairs of stars orbiting each other. While each pair eclipses its own two stars, as usual, only one pair eclipses the other. A paper outlining the properties of this unique system was submitted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 13. It has been accepted for publication in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How to CT scan a 400-pound crocodile
item.description: At 61, Bill had begun showing changes in his health—decreased appetite, weight loss and abdominal bloating. But his bloodwork was normal, leaving the cause of his symptoms unknown. The next step was clear: Bill should get a CT scan to check for problems with his internal organs. There was just one hurdle: Bill is a nearly 400-pound (approximately 180-kilogram) Siamese crocodile. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australia's bird flu response: Too little, but it's not too late
item.description: When news broke over the weekend that Australia's first mainland case of bird flu in a mammal—the death of a long-nosed fur seal—had been detected, I felt deep sadness and dread for what's likely to come next. We should expect large-scale deaths of mammals, in addition to birds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bird flu is spreading. Your backyard feeder could make it worse
item.description: Backyard bird feeders could become unexpected hotspots for H5N1 as Australia’s bird flu outbreak spreads, bringing species together in ways that rarely occur naturally. Experts say stopping feeding is safest, while smaller amounts of food, no hand-feeding, and careful cleaning can reduce the danger. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Meet Vick Tan: The Minnesota student who turned a teabag into a low-cost arsenic filter
item.description: In a groundbreaking initiative, a student has engineered a teabag designed to extract arsenic from polluted water. This clever pouch incorporates eggshells and magnetic iron oxide, successfully removing over ninety-eight percent of arsenic during rigorous laboratory assessments. Researchers are also investigating possibilities for its reuse and economical manufacturing. This innovation represents a significant leap towards providing accessible and safe drinking water. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: An AI job boom? Here's what the tedious, temporary work in data labeling is actually like
item.description: Amid all the talk about artificial intelligence (AI) both creating and destroying jobs, a troubling reality flies under the radar. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why hundreds of scientists want more protection for Australia's oceans
item.description: Australia is one of the world's great ocean nations. It is home to more marine species than any other country, with ocean ecosystems spanning all five of the world's climate zones, from the coral-rich tropics to the icy shores of Antarctica. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A ghostly ribbon of stars reveals hidden dark matter
item.description: A faint ribbon of stars around a distant galaxy has become the first globular cluster stellar stream ever identified beyond the Milky Way. Because the stars trace the galaxy’s gravity, researchers used the stream to estimate how much invisible dark matter surrounds it and how that matter is distributed. The breakthrough offers astronomers a promising new way to investigate one of the universe’s greatest mysteries. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A tiny “rainbow on a chip” could help supercharge 6G networks
item.description: Researchers have created a tiny chip that produces a stable “rainbow” of light capable of generating multiple high-frequency signals at once, potentially boosting the speed and capacity of future 6G networks. Its extreme precision could also make it valuable for quantum timing, navigation, radar, and even space-based technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Book Week is not just for big kids—how to engage babies and toddlers at story time
item.description: Book Week is a great opportunity for parents and caregivers to inspire a love of reading in babies and toddlers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Housing may shape death risks for low-income older renters
item.description: For low-income older adults, where they live may affect how long they live, according to new research from Washington University in St. Louis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
item.description: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Recycling meat waste may help bring cultivated meat to market
item.description: Researchers found microalgae can be grown using waste from cultivated meat production, then processed and fed back into the system, replacing some of the expensive ingredients needed to grow new meat cells. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds food insecurity remains in historically redlined neighborhoods
item.description: Bad housing, high crime and poor schools are more important than transportation or income when it comes to accessing healthy food in neighborhoods historically subjected to "redlining"—the now-illegal practice once used to refuse loans, insurance or mortgages to people in certain neighborhoods that were disproportionately inhabited by racial and ethnic minorities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Screen time at ages 1 and 6 may matter more than parents realize
item.description: More screen time during infancy and around the start of school was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later. The findings suggest that early childhood may contain particularly sensitive windows when screen habits can have longer-lasting effects. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China boosts coal’s economic value 700% after turning it to liquids: report
item.description: The world’s largest coal-to-liquids plant is turning coal into oil products that can power rockets and serve as machine lubricants while boosting its value sevenfold, according to a Chinese newspaper. The production line, built by China Energy Group Ningxia Coal Industry Co Ltd, began full operations in northwest China’s Ningxia Hui autonomous region last month and processed 24 million tonnes of coal in 2025 – a quarter of the region’s total annual output, according to a report published by... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Zhang Tong

item.title: Scientists just imaged the hidden quantum shape of a molecule
item.description: Researchers have found a way to create a complete 3D image of a molecule’s wavefunction, one of quantum mechanics’ most fundamental yet elusive features. By combining advanced photoelectron measurements with newly designed algorithms, the University of Göttingen team reconstructed the molecular orbital of a nanometer-sized organic molecule in remarkable detail, even resolving features smaller than the spacing between its carbon atoms. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Freezing liquid inside optical fibre makes light and sound interact 1,000 times more strongly
item.description: Scientists have frozen the liquid inside a special optical fibre to -196°C, creating conditions where light and sound interact more than 1,000 times more strongly than in ordinary fibres. The team found that the frozen fibre could still guide light and hypersonic sound waves. The breakthrough also helped researchers demonstrate optoacoustic memory, which could have potential applications in lower-energy photonic computing, quantum information processing and high-precision sensing. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Engineered yeasts help turn PET plastic and crop waste into protein-rich cookies
item.description: Plastic might be the last ingredient you would ever add to a cookie recipe. But a team of researchers is looking to change that. They've programmed yeasts to turn plastic and agricultural waste into edible proteins and flavoring molecules, creating a treat from trash. The technology not only offers a new upcycling method but could also sustain life in disaster zones or even deep-space missions with humans aboard. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nanoparticle flu vaccine protects against three influenza strains in mice
item.description: A new nanoparticle vaccine could one day give patients immunity to the flu with fewer trips to the doctor and without requiring health officials to correctly guess which flu strains will become dominant each year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Specialist ship arrives to cart SpaceX rocket from Christmas Island
item.description: A semi-submersible cargo carrier has arrived on the remote Australian territory to ferry the SpaceX starship back to Texas. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Watch live: MTG-I2 set for liftoff
item.description: The next Meteosat Third Generation Imager satellite (MTG-I2) is set for liftoff on flight VA270 on an Ariane 6, from Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana. It will complete the first family of MTG satellites, which will deliver data for weather forecasting over Europe and northern Africa in unprecedented detail. The launch will be broadcast on Thursday, 27 August, on ESA WebTV. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Massachusetts crew lands 1,260-pound blue marlin, misses world record
item.description: In a thrilling encounter off Cape Cod, a charter captain teamed up with an angler to reel in an astonishing blue marlin that tipped the scales at 1,260 pounds and stretched over eleven feet. This remarkable catch approached the Atlantic blue marlin world record from 1992, prompting researchers to investigate its head to gauge its age. After the impressive capture, the fish was generously shared among several admirers. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Washington releases 20 lab-raised sunflower stars to restore kelp forests
item.description: In a remarkable conservation initiative, twenty lab-raised sunflower sea stars have been released back into the Salish Sea. This effort seeks to restore a species that has suffered extensively due to disease, crucial for the health of kelp forest ecosystems. The project, undertaken in collaboration with the Samish Indian Nation and various researchers, symbolizes hope for restoring ecological balance in the region. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: China says unmanned moon mission delayed over 'launch conditions'
item.description: China's manned space agency said Sunday it is delaying a research moon mission that is part of Beijing's efforts to land a crew there by 2030, less than two weeks after a rare launch failure. Publicado también por: The Times of India - World. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ‘An amazing relief’: implant offers hope for those with refractory angina
item.description: Study finds device brings significant fall in chest pain in 75% of patients, but further trials and NHS approval are needed “It’s an amazing relief, both physically and emotionally, to be able to live my life again normally, without feeling that I’m limited all the time in what I can do.” Cristian Jensen is describing the difference that an implant inserted in his chest – to reduce the symptoms of his debilitating angina – has had on his life. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Denis Campbell Health policy editor

item.title: NASA is about to launch a powerful new eye on the universe
item.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has been cleared for final launch preparations ahead of a targeted August 30 liftoff aboard SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy. The powerful new observatory will probe cosmic expansion, the history of the universe, and distant exoplanets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Trump to award Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II astronauts
item.description: The Artemis II crew will receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor after becoming the first humans in more than 50 years to travel beyond the Moon. Their 10-day Orion mission also carried them farther into space than anyone in history. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: What Lake Bonneville Left Behind
item.description: The drying of the massive lake exposed playas that became the setting for feats of engineering and technological ingenuity, as well as epic tales of exploration and desperation. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists discover a real-life “dragon” and name it after Syrax
item.description: Scientists discovered a small, yellowish mountain horned dragon in Thailand and named it Acanthosaura syrax after a dragon from House of the Dragon. Found only in a narrow band of high-elevation forest, the distinctive new species could become a flagship for protecting its rare mountain habitat. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Gut bacteria may unlock a hidden benefit of vegetables
item.description: Gut bacteria can transform nitrate and plant-based iron from vegetables and other foods into protective molecules that may benefit the heart and metabolism. In experimental models, higher levels of these compounds were linked to lower blood pressure, better blood sugar control, healthier blood vessels, and less liver fat. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: Tens of thousands of years ago, the Great Barrier Reef was above water. Whether it was grassland, rainforest, or mangrove swamp is something researchers and Indigenous rangers are trying to uncover. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Protein degradation rate helps explain why humans develop more slowly than mice
item.description: Humans develop at a slower rate than other mammalian species, like mice, but scientists are still trying to understand the molecular basis of these differences. Now, researchers from the Ebisuya Group at EMBL Barcelona and PoL-TU Dresden and from the Savitski Team at EMBL Heidelberg show that across 4,000 proteins shared between humans and mice, there is a clear tendency for protein degradation in humans to be slower than in mice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Collaborative drawing offers new insights into how strangers become friends
item.description: The closer two people grow, the more alike their brains work—or so the assumption goes. Two ETH Zurich studies challenge this idea by examining the brain activity of younger and older adults who drew together over several weeks. Despite growing closer, the similarity of their brain activity did not simply increase. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2020, Phoenix coated 36 miles of roads to fight extreme heat; surfaces became 12°F cooler at noon
item.description: Phoenix has implemented a reflective coating on its roads to mitigate urban heat island effects, effectively reducing asphalt temperatures during daylight hours. However, researchers observed that this treatment inadvertently intensified heat radiation exposure for pedestrians in close proximity. They concluded that incorporating shade from trees and buildings is essential for enhancing human comfort, suggesting cities explore a variety of solutions beyond just reflective coatings to address rising temperatures. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists left this farm field alone. Thousands of orchids appeared
item.description: An abandoned farm field became a flourishing wildflower meadow within little more than a decade, with plant diversity doubling and thousands of orchids appearing naturally. The discovery suggests that simply giving nature time to recover could be a powerful and inexpensive tool for restoring biodiversity. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Spying device detectors may give domestic abuse victims false sense of security, study finds
item.description: Many tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillance Commercial detectors intended to help domestic abuse victims find hidden spying devices may actually give them a false sense of security, a study has found. The consumer detection tools claim to identify hidden cameras, microphones or trackers through methods such as signal-strength readings, infrared lens detection and scanning for wifi or Bluetooth devices. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: JWST peeks at Callisto's ancient scars
item.description: Of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, Callisto is the one that gets the least attention. Io is constantly being resurfaced by volcanoes. Europa has a giant liquid water ocean. And Ganymede has its own magnetic field that interacts with its parent planet in weird ways. Callisto, by comparison, seems sedate, with its ancient, crater-saturated surface seemingly frozen in time. But new data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) shows that even this most benign of the Big Four moons is more active than previously realized. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hot temperatures can dull blue morpho butterflies' iridescent scales
item.description: Blue morpho butterflies have captivated the human eye for centuries. We even have one as an emoji on our phones. In a recent experiment, researchers at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) documented for the first time that hot temperatures during development can reduce the brightness of their iridescence. At hot temperatures, such as those projected in future warming scenarios, the structures responsible for their iridescent color could change enough that common bird predators and other butterflies of the same species would likely see a color change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: China said on Sunday it was postponing its planned ambitious Chang'e-7 lunar mission, which was set to carry out explorations including searching for water ice on the moon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The dental crown of the future could be 3D-printed while you wait
item.description: Researchers have found a way to slash the processing time for 3D-printed zirconia crowns from as much as 100 hours to under 30 minutes. The advance could eventually let dentists print strong, customized permanent crowns for patients within a single appointment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: The superconducting gap of an ultrathin nickelate defies expectations
item.description: Superconductors are materials that carry electrical current with zero resistance below a specific critical temperature. In conventional superconductors, the transition to superconductivity generally occurs at very low temperatures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Your backyard could hold a rare earth fortune – and this orange lichen is the clue
item.description: Next time you spot a vivid orange-yellow crust spreading across a rock in your garden, on a country wall or along a hiking trail, take a closer look – you might be standing on a fortune. A Chinese research team has found that a humble lichen could serve as a visible field indicator of unknown rare earth deposits around the world. The researchers said the lichen’s distinctive colour made it easy to spot on exposed rock, and the discovery could be combined with unmanned aerial vehicles and... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Physicists create a tiny “Big Bang” with surprisingly small atomic nuclei
item.description: Researchers at CERN have created microscopic versions of the early Universe by colliding surprisingly small atomic nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The collisions produced quark-gluon plasma, the ultra-hot matter believed to have filled the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Even more intriguingly, the particles left behind reveal the shape of the nuclei that created them, offering a new way to probe both nuclear physics and the Universe’s earliest moments. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
